How to compost at home

By Dr Maya Okonkwo, updated 1 September 2026

Home composting is the process of turning kitchen scraps and garden waste into a dark, crumbly soil conditioner using naturally occurring bacteria and fungi. A well-managed heap produces usable compost in 8 to 12 weeks, and diverts roughly 150 kg of waste per household each year, according to the 2025 WRAP household waste survey.

What can I put in a compost heap?

A compost heap needs a rough balance of two materials. Greens supply nitrogen and are wet; browns supply carbon and are dry. Aim for about 50% of each by volume.

  • Greens: vegetable peelings, coffee grounds, grass clippings, tea leaves
  • Browns: cardboard, dry leaves, straw, shredded paper, wood chip
  • Avoid: cooked food, meat, dairy, diseased plants, perennial weed roots

How long does compost take to make?

A hot heap turned weekly produces finished compost in 8 to 12 weeks. A cold heap that is never turned takes 9 to 12 months. The difference is oxygen: turning reintroduces air, which lets aerobic bacteria work roughly 20 times faster than the anaerobic ones that take over in a compacted heap.

Composting methods compared
MethodTime to finishEffort
Hot heap, turned weekly8–12 weeksHigh

Why has my compost stopped working?

A stalled heap almost always has one of three causes. Too wet and it goes anaerobic and smells of ammonia. Too dry and the bacteria go dormant. Too much brown material and there is not enough nitrogen to fuel decomposition.

The fix for a wet heap is to add shredded cardboard and turn it. The fix for a dry heap is to water it until it feels like a wrung-out sponge. Both changes typically restore activity within a week.

Is compost safe for growing vegetables?

Finished home compost is safe for vegetable beds provided the heap reached at least 55°C for three consecutive days, which kills most pathogens and weed seeds. The UK government composting guidance and the National Institutes of Health both note that cold heaps may not reach this threshold, so compost from an unturned heap is better used on ornamental beds.

Frequently asked questions

Can I compost in winter?

Yes, though decomposition slows below 10°C. Insulating the heap with cardboard maintains activity.

Do I need a compost bin?

No. An open heap works, but a bin retains heat and moisture, cutting the time to finished compost by roughly a third.

How do I know when compost is ready?

Finished compost is dark brown, crumbly, and smells of woodland soil. No original ingredient should be recognisable.
